title: Through my fault
hook: the whole church admits it has sinned and asks each other for prayer

segments.voice: Yesterday, the entrance: a procession, a kissed altar, a greeting. Your line was we gather first.

A staff meeting begins. Everyone stands up, the boss included, and says out loud, together: I've messed up. In what I thought, what I said, what I did, and what I didn't do. It's my fault. Then everyone turns to the people around them and says: please pray for me. It would be the strangest meeting of the year. And it's roughly what can happen in the first minutes of a Catholic Mass. Right after the greeting, before a single reading, the whole church owns up.
screen: `A MEETING THAT STARTS WITH SORRY.` → `EVERYONE, THE BOSS INCLUDED.` → `THE FIRST MINUTES OF MASS.`

segments.voice: It's called the Confiteor, from its first word in Latin: I confess. The priest invites everyone to call their sins to mind, and there's a short silence. Then priest and people together say they confess to almighty God, and to each other, that they have greatly sinned, in their thoughts and in their words, in what they have done and in what they have failed to do. That last part is sharp: not just the wrong things, but the good things left undone. Then comes the line, in the old Latin: mea culpa, mea culpa, mea maxima culpa. Through my fault, through my fault, through my most grievous fault. As they say it, people strike their chest with a closed hand. That gesture echoes a story Jesus told. A tax collector stands at the back of the Temple, won't even lift his eyes, beats his breast and says, in the Douay-Rheims: "O God, be merciful to me a sinner." Jesus says that man went home right with God. Then the Confiteor turns outward. Everyone asks Mary, the angels and the saints, and you, my brothers and sisters, to pray for me. You confess to the people beside you, and then you ask them for help. Nobody stands above anybody; the priest says it too. The Church is clear that this isn't the sacrament of confession, and doesn't replace it. It's a way of starting honestly. Looking back over this week, from bending the knee to the Angelus to the entrance, the body keeps saying things before words do. Here, it's a fist on the chest.
screen: `CONFITEOR: I CONFESS.` · `DONE, AND FAILED TO DO.` · `MEA CULPA, AND A FIST ON THE CHEST.` · `PRAY FOR ME, BROTHERS AND SISTERS.` · then, large: `O GOD, BE MERCIFUL TO ME A SINNER.`

segments.voice: Look back over the last day or two, not to punish yourself, just to see clearly: one thing you did that you wish you hadn't, one thing you left undone. If you're Catholic, or you'd like to, you can strike your chest gently, once, the way the tax collector did, and if you pray, you can use his words. If not, just name it, and set it down.
Confiteor. I confess: the prayer at the start of Mass where everyone admits their sins and asks each other for prayer.
Your line: we all begin as sinners. The priest and the whole church start Mass with the same words: my fault. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: At the start of most Masses, after a brief silence, priest and people pray the Confiteor together, many striking their breast at 'through my fault'; it is one of several forms of the penitential act and does not replace the sacrament of confession.

chat.says: Why do people tap their chest during the prayer at the start of Mass?
options: They strike the chest at through my fault, like the tax collector asking mercy.
It's to show they're sorry for other people's sins, not their own.
It's a small sign of the cross, for when the church is too crowded.
chat.meaning: In the Confiteor, people strike the chest at mea culpa, echoing the tax collector who beat his breast and asked for mercy.
